A partial derivative of a multivariable function is its derivative with respect to one variable while holding all other variables constant. It measures the rate at which the function changes along the direction of a coordinate axis in multivariable space. Partial derivatives are the fundamental building blocks of multivariable calculus, differential geometry, and mathematical physics.

Formally, the partial derivative of f of x, y with respect to x at the point a, b is defined as the limit of the difference quotient f of a plus h, b minus f of a, b, all over h, as h approaches zero. You can denote this with the curly-d notation, the partial-derivative symbol ∂, as in ∂f over ∂x, or by subscripts such as f subscript x. The curly-d symbol was introduced by Adrien-Marie Legendre and later popularized by Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi.

When second-order partial derivatives are continuous, Clairaut's theorem, also called Schwarz's theorem, tells us that the mixed partial derivatives are equal. In other words, the partial derivative with respect to x and then y equals the partial derivative with respect to y and then x.

First-order partial derivatives are collected into the gradient vector, written as del f, which points in the direction of the greatest rate of increase of the function. In vector calculus, the Jacobian matrix is the matrix of all first-order partial derivatives of a vector-valued function. It represents the best linear approximation to the function at a point and is essential for understanding how multivariable functions behave locally.

Partial derivatives extend the single-variable derivative concept to multiple dimensions. Partial differential equations, or PDEs, are differential equations that contain partial derivatives and model phenomena ranging from heat diffusion to wave propagation. When optimizing multivariable functions, you find critical points by setting all partial derivatives to zero.
